title: Infrastructure, SaaS replacement, websites, and online stores
questions: What services does Anthony offer?
Can you build a self-hosted system?
Do you do websites, online stores, or custom consulting?
text: Anthony Bluemel builds client-owned open-source infrastructure, helps replace SaaS tools, designs business websites, and implements online stores and commerce integrations. For infrastructure, he sizes the deployment, secures and connects the agreed tools, and trains the team that will run them. You pay a one-time implementation fee and buy hardware, hosting, and third-party services in your own name. You can also describe a custom consulting request in the project brief so Anthony can confirm scope.

title: What the one-time fee covers
questions: What is included in the project fee?
Is this a monthly managed service?
What will I pay Anthony for?
text: Anthony agrees on the work and acceptance checks before implementation. The infrastructure quote covers the agreed deployment, integrations, migration, recovery checks, and training, with application modules and migration itemized. The statement of work specifies the one-time price and deliverables. You pay providers for hardware, hosting, and third-party services through your own accounts. Your designated operator handles routine maintenance after handoff.

title: Standard Infrastructure pricing and scope
questions: What does Standard cost?
Can I start with one server?
Can you deploy without Kubernetes?
text: Standard Infrastructure is a non-HA deployment with a one-time professional services planning range of $3,000 to $6,000 USD. It suits smaller businesses or internal applications that can tolerate a host outage. Anthony typically uses one VPS or physical host, with Docker Compose by default or lightweight K3s when the workload calls for it. The scope includes single-instance databases, monitoring and alerts, TLS and access controls, automated offsite backups, documented recovery, AI-assisted troubleshooting, and administrator training. Anthony itemizes application modules and migration in the project quote.

title: High Availability Infrastructure pricing and scope
questions: What does HA cost?
Can you build a redundant cluster?
Can the system survive a server failure?
text: High Availability Infrastructure has a one-time professional services planning range of $8,000 to $15,000+ USD. Anthony designs redundancy around agreed recovery goals using managed Kubernetes with an HA control plane or a custom self-managed architecture. The scope can include multiple workers, workload replication and failover where supported, database clustering, redundant routing, and persistent storage designed for each workload. It includes GitOps, monitoring and alerts, incident runbooks, offsite backups, restore tests, and AI-assisted troubleshooting. Anthony confirms which failures and user workflows the deployment should handle.

title: Uptime, downtime, and failover
questions: Does Kubernetes guarantee uptime?
Can you guarantee zero downtime?
How much data could we lose?
text: Availability depends on the whole path users need, including identity, ingress, databases, storage, and the application. Tell Anthony which workflows need to keep running, how long you can wait for recovery, and how much recent data you could afford to lose. Anthony uses that to scope the architecture and recovery checks. Uptime and recovery commitments require project-specific agreement.

title: Hosting choices and purchase brief
questions: Can I use hardware I already have?
Can you use a VPS or my cloud account?
Who buys the hardware?
text: You can use existing equipment, purchase bare metal, rent a VPS, or use managed Kubernetes where suitable. Anthony sizes the system around users, storage growth, uptime, and recovery goals. He prepares a purchase brief covering equipment or cloud resources and who administers them. You order equipment or open the provider accounts and control billing.

title: Recurring costs and software licenses
questions: Is self-hosting free after the project?
Is there a per-user fee?
Will I save money compared with SaaS?
text: The agreed open-source stack carries no per-seat license fee and the implementation has no recurring fee to Anthony. Budget for infrastructure, backups, administration, and any optional paid provider services, extensions, or maintenance you arrange. Each upstream package keeps its license. Use the calculator to compare your actual commercial subscription costs with self-hosting estimates over one, three, or five years. Savings depend on your inputs.

title: Planning estimates and formal quote
questions: Can you quote my project here?
Is the calculator total a firm price?
Can you do it for my budget?
text: The pricing ranges and calculator totals are planning estimates in USD. The calculator lets you enter your own costs and carry a summary into the project brief. Anthony sets the implementation price after reviewing the workload, applications, migration, and acceptance checks. The statement of work governs the final price.

title: Application module planning ranges
questions: How much does one application cost?
Are app integrations included in the infrastructure price?
text: The one-time USD implementation ranges are $500 to $1,500 for a simple standalone application, $1,500 to $3,000 for intermediate work that needs integration or extra validation, and $3,000 to $10,000+ for a complex business system with more workflows or extensive configuration. Anthony checks the edition, dependencies, and compatibility. He quotes migration, cloud services, subscriptions, and paid features separately from application implementation.

title: Application selection and SaaS replacement
questions: Can I replace Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace?
Which products can you deploy?
Can you help pick CRM, ERP, or helpdesk software?
text: Start with the workflows your team needs to keep. The catalog includes Nextcloud for files and calendars, EuroOffice for browser-based document editing, Nextcloud Talk and Jitsi Meet for calls, SuiteCRM for sales, Odoo Community and ERPNext for business operations, Zammad for helpdesk, Forgejo for Git collaboration, and Medusa for headless commerce. Use the Replacement Map to compare features, who runs each option, and costs. Confirm the edition, sign-in and integrations, export coverage, maintenance, and recovery needs during discovery.

title: Migration and cutover
questions: Can you move my existing data?
Can we migrate with no downtime?
Is migration included?
text: Anthony can scope a migration and itemize it in the quote. Share the source tools, approximate data volume, required history and attachments, and how much cutover downtime the team can accept. The available exports, import compatibility, required workflows, and project scope determine what can move and how to check the result.

title: Client ownership of accounts, code, and data
questions: Who owns the system?
Can I bring in another provider later?
Do I get administrator access?
text: Your business controls provider billing, domains, administrator access, the deployment repository, configuration, runbooks, data exports, and backup access. You own hardware you purchase. Your provider owns rented hardware. You can take your project files to another operator under the applicable upstream software licenses.

title: Handoff deliverables and acceptance checks
questions: What do I receive at handoff?
How will I know the project is finished?
Do you document the deployment?
text: Anthony agrees on acceptance checks with you before the build. Your named administrator uses client credentials to check access, rotate a temporary deployment credential, identify the production version and its repository, and restore and verify a sample file in a separate folder. The handoff also covers architecture and deployment instructions, backup retention and recovery targets, an update and rollback rehearsal in an agreed test environment, and checking an AI troubleshooting recommendation against the cited runbook.

title: Maintenance, training, and support after handoff
questions: Who runs it after you leave?
Do I need a dedicated IT team?
Can I get ongoing support or 24/7 on-call?
text: Your designated operator handles routine updates, access, monitoring, and recovery checks with the runbooks Anthony provides. Anthony trains the operator on the agreed stack. Additional training has a one-time planning range of $750 to $2,000 USD. Ask Anthony directly to discuss any post-handoff support, response times, or on-call coverage.

title: Backups and restore practice
questions: Do you set up offsite backups?
Can I test that my backups work?
Is the restore demo real?
text: Anthony scopes backups around protected data, retention, recovery goals, and the backup destination. Your operator practices recovering a sample file using your own credentials and verifies the copy before replacing anything. The online restore exercise uses simulated snapshots and a sample runbook. A project’s acceptance checks apply to the environment you receive.

title: Sign-in and private access
questions: Can we have SSO, VPN, or HTTPS?
Can we keep internal apps private?
Can we use our existing identity provider?
text: Anthony scopes TLS, private access, network segmentation, and roles around who needs each application. Centralized authentication depends on the application’s supported integration and role mapping. Share which users need access, which apps should be public or private, and any existing sign-in system during discovery.

title: AI-assisted operations and expanded setup
questions: Can my team use local AI to troubleshoot?
Will AI make changes automatically?
How much is the expanded AI assistant?
text: Anthony hands over an AI troubleshooting assistant that uses approved runbooks and diagnostics for your deployment. Your administrator checks the evidence and approves production actions through the usual auditable change workflow. A self-hosted model is an option where practical. The expanded setup for additional diagnostic and documentation sources has a one-time planning range of $1,500 to $4,000 USD. Your business controls the model environment and pays any provider charges.

title: Preparing and sending a project brief
questions: How do I get started?
Can I book a consultation?
What should I send for a quote?
text: Choose infrastructure deployment, SaaS replacement, website development, e-commerce development, or custom consulting in the project brief. Describe your current tools, what you want to change, and who will run the system. Include hosting preferences, an application or calculator summary, migration needs, or a target date if relevant. The browser prepares an email draft or lets you copy the brief. You send it from your email app to antblu@antblu.net.

title: Timeline and project availability
questions: When can you start?
How long will it take?
Can you finish by my deadline?
text: Share your target date, purchase lead times if known, and any cutover windows in the project brief. Anthony can discuss timing once he understands the applications, dependencies, migration, and acceptance checks.

title: Antalos reference infrastructure
questions: What is Antalos?
Can I see how Anthony builds infrastructure?
Do I need to run the full Antalos stack?
text: Antalos is Anthony's reference template for self-hosted applications and VMs. The public handbook shows the lab design and the Services inventory includes tools and archived templates. The dashboard screenshots capture a point in time. The Emiliany case study shows a bilingual storefront and how Anthony connected orders, accounts, email preferences, and support. The application tour and restore exercise let you explore examples. Anthony selects your topology and applications based on your requirements.

title: Website and online store implementation
questions: Do you build websites and online stores?
Which service should I choose for my business?
text: Choose web development for a landing page or a multi-page business site. Choose e-commerce development for a store that needs a catalog, checkout, and order management or for a custom commerce platform with cross-system workflows. Anthony deploys the project in your accounts and trains your team. Use the relevant service page for starting prices or prepare a project brief for the scope you need.

title: Illustrative monthly hosting costs
questions: How much does hosting cost per month?
What should I budget for my hardware, a VPS, or managed Kubernetes?
text: The Infrastructure page lists three illustrative monthly allowances in USD. Customer-owned hardware has a $20 to $150 power and connectivity allowance, with equipment, backups, and labor budgeted separately. A cloud VPS has a $30 to $300 compute allowance before workload storage, backups, and networking. Managed Kubernetes has a $150 to $800 cluster allowance. Region, control plane, nodes, ingress, and storage affect that total. Anthony sizes the resources for your workload before you order.

title: Comparing subscription and self-hosting costs
questions: How do I use the cost calculator?
Can I estimate break-even or share the estimate?
text: Compare commercial and self-hosted total costs over one, three, or five years. Replace sample prices with your actual bills and enter your expected implementation, applications, migration, hardware or hosting, backup and other running costs, and administrator labor. The tool can show break-even when the scenarios are comparable. Copy the estimate or carry its summary to the project brief. The totals help you plan and depend on the costs you enter.

title: Landing Page and Business Website packages
questions: How much does a landing page cost?
What does a business website include?
Can I edit my site after launch?
text: A Landing Page starts at $900 USD for a responsive single page with a contact form, basic SEO, performance optimization, deployment, and handoff. A Business Website starts at $2,500 USD and typically covers five to eight responsive pages, contact forms, basic SEO and performance optimization, optional CMS integration on request, and administrator training. Anthony confirms the final page count and quotes extra pages and custom work separately. You keep your domain, hosting, source, and content exports. Your team practices publishing a change and restoring an earlier version. Budget separately for hosting, domain registration, and optional maintenance.

title: Standard E-commerce Store and Custom E-commerce Platform packages
questions: How much does a standard online store cost?
Can you build a headless store or integrate our ERP?
Who owns the payment account?
text: A Standard E-commerce Store starts at $5,000 USD for a storefront, catalog and cart, checkout and payments, basic shipping and tax setup, order management, and administrator training. A Custom E-commerce Platform starts at $10,000 USD and can include headless commerce, custom APIs and storefronts, CRM or ERP integration, inventory synchronization, and advanced account or fulfillment workflows. Advanced projects can exceed $25,000 USD. You control the store, hosting, domain, and payment provider accounts. Your team checks a sample order and exports records during handoff. Budget separately for processing fees, hosting, domains, optional extensions, and maintenance.
